catalog_quote: After analysing all available evidence, Maggi comes to the conclusion that Old Khotanese was a language with a 'quasi-fixed' stress. In general, he argues, the stress in polysyllables fell on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word (other than the final syllable, which was never stressed), while words containing only light syllables were stressed on the initial syllable. However, these rules are not absolute, hence the qualification 'quasi-'. In particular, Maggi states that words of four or more syllables with the abl. sg. m. ending -äna or the loc. pl. ending -uvŏ' are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable, even if this is light. ... [p. 21:] it is clear from Maggi 1992, §94, that metrical considerations provide the only evidence for his statement that the heavy final syllable of a polysyllabic word is never accented. ... new_statements.quote: [p. 343] Some of these are generally accepted, e.g. … that the final light syllable of a polysyllabic word never bears the stress. Others may be less than universally accepted, e.g. that many words of more than two syllables have both primary and secondary stress. [p. 344] A large majority of these end with a word of the shape HL or LHL, e.g. balysa ‘Buddhas’ or yanīmä ‘I do’, a few in longer words ending °LHL, all of which are probably (though not in all cases demonstrably) stressed on the heavy penultimate syllable °ˈHL (in accordance with the rule stated by Maggi 1992: 52, §80; Emmerick 2024: 9, §1.15).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Old Khotanese has an empty rule field, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: weight-sensitive right-edge stress (heavy penult; final light syllable never stressed) with morphologically conditioned initial stress in finite verbs and secondary stress in longer words. Nothing in the catalog to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weight-sensitive and counted from the right edge: a word-final light syllable is never stressed, and words ending .HL or..LHL (the vast majority) carry the stress on the heavy penult (the Maggi 1992 / Emmerick 2024 rule: stress on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word, excluding the final). Sims-Williams reconstructs the system from metrical lightening: a heavy syllable that can be metrically lightened must be unstressed, so uysnōra HHL is HˈHL, handara HLL is HˈLL, aysmū HH is HˈH (he suggests all HH words may be stressed on the second syllable). Morphologically conditioned stem-initial stress overrides the weight rule in finite verb forms: ˈsarbīndä ˈHHL ‘they rise’, ˈsarbätĕ ˈHLL, ˈkṣamätä ˈLLL (the 3 sg. pres. of many type-A verbs), contrasted with häˈmätĕ ‘becomes’; he calls these ‘a more general set of rules regarding the stress of finite verbal forms’ (Sims-Williams 2022: 76-77). Unlike Emmerick he holds (per the Reader preface, held by the project) that final syllables with a long vowel or diphthong can be stressed (thaˈtau vs Emmerick’s ˈthato).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: ‘many words of more than two syllables have both primary and secondary stress’ (p. 343) and ‘longer words have a secondary stress on which the an earlier reading may fall’ (p. 354); the metrical an earlier reading may coincide with either the primary or a secondary word-stress (n. 6, p. 333).
new_statements.exceptions: Finite verb forms with a heavy monosyllabic present/past stem plus HL ending (ˈsarbīndä) and 3 sg. pres. forms of type-A verbs (ˈkṣamätä ˈLLL, ˈsarbätĕ ˈHLL) are stressed on the first syllable, not the heavy penult; hīṣṭātĕ HHL ‘he sent’ lightens to hìṣṭātĕ LHL because the stress falls on the root *stā (two merged verbs), unlike pyūṣṭāndä; ˈuysanV̆ ‘breath’ has initial stress on the preverb (< *úz-anā-) contrasting with the cognate verb; English ˈadult ~ aˈdult cited as a parallel for doublets (n. 39, p. 352). The whole reconstruction is presented as a hypothesis inferred from metre, disputed by Fattori 2025 and Hitch 2014/2024, who deny that stress is a structural feature of the metre.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Old Khotanese as attested in the Book of Zambasta (5th-6th c. CE, Khotan); Sims-Williams reconstructs ‘the system of word-stress in the language of the author’ of Z. Late Khotanese forms (LKhot. ˈhime, uysaṃdī) are cited only as comparative evidence. Emmerick’s Handbook rule is stated for Khotanese generally.

readall_conflicts: Within the opened material there is one substantive disagreement about placement and one about the status of stress. (1) Placement at the right edge: Emmerick’s Handbook rule (2024: 9, §1.15-1.16, publisher sample held by the project) says stress falls on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word ‘but not on the final syllable itself’, and words with no non-final heavy syllable are stressed on the first syllable (ˈpharu, ˈthato, ˈhvatana); Sims-Williams (Reader preface, and the 2025 IIJ article) accepts the heavy-penult rule for..HL words and that a final light syllable is never stressed, but holds that all or most words ending in a syllable with a long vowel or diphthong are stressed on that final syllable (thaˈtau, aysˈmū HˈH), and that finite verb forms such as ˈsarbīndä, ˈkṣamätä, ˈsarbätĕ carry stem-initial stress regardless of weight. (2) Status: Fattori 2025 and Hitch 2014/2024, as reported by Sims-Williams, deny that word stress is a structural feature of Old Khotanese metre and hold the metre to be purely quantitative; Sims-Williams notes that Fattori nonetheless ‘seems inclined to accept that the difference between these two classes of HHL words was probably a matter of stress’ (n. 22, p. 343). All parties agree the language had a word stress; the dispute is over its exact position in certain word classes and whether the metre tracks it. The Dragoni review could not be opened, so its position is unknown.

sources.quote: §1.15 'Khotanese had a stress accent that lay on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word but not on the final syllable itself. A heavy syllable is defined as a syllable containing a long or nasalised vowel or a syllable ending in one or more consonants. Thus, yanīmä /jaˈniːmə/ ... is stressed on the penult ... because it contains the long vowel ī, while namaśtä /naˈmaštə/ ... is stressed on the penult because it ends in the consonant ś.' §1.16 'Words containing no heavy syllables or whose only heavy syllable is their final syllable are stressed on the first syllable e.g. pharu /ˈpʰar
